title: The true cost of an unfilled shift
description: While traditional strategies for addressing staffing gaps get the job done, they don’t address the underlying problem.
content:
Ask a facility operator what an unfilled nursing shift costs, and they’ll tell you the coverage cost, the overtime rate or whatever a third-party staffing agency charged for last-minute support. Those figures are easy to track because they’re connected to an invoice, but they only reflect a small part of the actual cost.
While these traditional strategies for addressing staffing gaps get the job done, they don’t address the underlying problem. The same shortfall continues on repeat, only to receive the same patchwork solution over and over again. It’s a costly narrative when matched against the staffing headwinds in today’s long-term care facilities.
Consider how this model creates additional costs for a facility operator. The first shows up in who absorbs the gap. When a shortfall gets patched with overtime, the same core staff pick up the difference, week after week. Repeated, unplanned overtime of that kind is one of the more reliable predictors of who eventually walks away from a job or nursing career.
The gap this creates leaves the facility paying higher agency rates for months while it backfills the vacancy. Add to that the costs of recruiting and training a full-time replacement, and a simple scheduling decision has turned into a turnover expense.
There are additional risks associated with unstable and unpredictable staffing patterns that can create long-term impacts on costs and reputation.
For example, when regulatory surveyors arrive unexpectedly, a bad day for staffing can turn into a citation that negatively impacts the facility’s star rating. Staffing gaps can have a potentially devastating impact on a facility’s ability to attract and retain new residents or patients. For years, leaders in the long-term care space managed that risk by predicting when surveys would happen and preparing teams accordingly. A 2025 National Bureau of Economic Research study documented that staffing and RN hours would rise in the days ahead of a survey, then fall back within weeks of the survey team leaving.
Solutions for today’s staffing gaps
That’s not the case today. Newer survey rules are closing the window, allowing longer onsite stretches and less predictable off-hour start times. Facilities have fewer chances to stage a good day and risk exposure from staffing gaps.
Turnover and survey exposure aren’t separate problems from the coverage cost. They come from the same unresolved gap, and operators keep paying to patch it instead of closing it permanently.
None of this means overtime or supplemental staffing is the enemy. Every facility uses both, and they should. The mistake is viewing those costs through the lens of an invoice only, rather than considering the bigger picture.
A better solution comes in the form of flexible staffing models that anticipate variability instead of scrambling based on last-minute availability. In practice, this means blending full-time staff with a predictable layer of flexible clinicians, often through a roster of trusted per-diem nurses who’ve worked with an organization before and already know its workflows and team fit. Over time, these clinicians become familiar faces rather than strangers walking onto the unit, so shifts run more smoothly.
The true cost of an unfilled shift is never a single invoice. It’s the burnout from repeated overtime, the months of elevated agency rates after a resignation, and the citation and reputational risk when staffing gaps meet an unannounced survey.
The fix isn’t eliminating overtime or supplemental staffing but building a better staffing model so coverage gaps get closed instead of endlessly patched.
Curtis Anderson is the founder and CEO of Nursa, a nationwide platform that enables skilled nursing facilities, hospitals, health systems and community organizations to secure reliable, qualified nursing talent for per diem shifts and contract work.

title: The business of better mealtimes: Dysphagia management in skilled nursing
description: Dysphagia management is an opportunity for the care team to collaborate and improve care.
content:
For many nursing home residents, meals are among the most meaningful moments of the day. Mealtimes are also moments when clinical risk, care coordination and resident choice converge.
A successful mealtime depends on far more than what is on the tray. It depends on whether residents can participate as independently as possible, whether their preferences are understood, and whether care teams have a clear, consistent plan for providing that person-centered level of support.
Small decisions about positioning, pacing, supervision and diet consistencies can shape both the resident experience and clinical outcomes.
Swallowing difficulty, or dysphagia, is one important part of that larger picture. When swallowing concerns arise, an effective response requires more than a change to the diet order. Speech-language pathologists, or SLPs, can help the interdisciplinary team assess the concern and develop practical, individualized recommendations that can be carried out consistently across shifts.
Dysphagia management is an opportunity for the care team to collaborate and improve care.
When the processes around mealtimes are unclear, the consequences can extend beyond the dining room. A resident may remain on a restrictive diet longer than necessary, affecting quality of life and potentially adding avoidable costs to the facility for thickened liquids.
Inconsistent approaches across shifts can also make it harder for residents to eat and drink enough to maintain their weight, sometimes contributing to the need for avoidable nutritional supplements.
Families may have questions about why a loved one’s eating experience has changed and receive different answers. The care team may be making high-stakes decisions without the objective information needed to feel confident in its plan.
When to call in support
A clear referral process can help teams respond before uncertainty becomes a larger problem. The American Speech-Language Hearing Association’s (ASHA) Guidelines for Referring to Speech-Language Pathology Services in Skilled Nursing Facilities offers a practical checklist for nursing and other care team members to identify signs that trigger an SLP referral.
After referral, the SLP can determine the appropriate next step, which may include a clinical bedside swallowing assessment and, when indicated, instrumental assessment.
An SLP’s clinical bedside swallowing assessment — evaluating a resident’s medical history and factors like alertness, breathing and fatigue as they eat, drink and use swallowing strategies — is a foundational part of dysphagia care. It provides important information about the resident’s symptoms, functional abilities, preferences, and response to strategies during a real mealtime context.
The clinical bedside assessment helps the SLP identify swallowing concerns, make initial care recommendations and determine if an instrumental assessment or other testing is needed. Instrumental swallowing assessments are the only way to actually see how swallowing works inside the body.
Two common options of instrumental assessments are fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES), which uses a small flexible camera to view swallowing at the bedside, and a videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS), an X-ray study that is typically completed outside of the facility. Together, these assessment approaches help the SLP and care team make individualized recommendations based on the resident’s needs and the information available.
Creating a practical plan
For SNF leaders, access to instrumental assessments is an important care-delivery decision. Some facilities may support an in-house FEES program, while others may rely on a contracted mobile FEES provider or a referral relationship for VFSS.
The important question is whether the SLP and interdisciplinary team can obtain timely information when needed and translate the results into practical, individualized plans that care teams can carry out consistently.
ASHA’s Making a Case: Instrumental Swallowing Assessments offers talking points that can help leaders and SLPs connect access to instrumental assessment with facility priorities. For organizations exploring an in-house approach, Getting Started With Flexible Endoscopic Evaluation of Swallowing (FEES) outlines considerations related to state and facility requirements, competency, training, equipment and team processes.
SLPs then help connect assessment findings with real-world mealtime implementation: positioning, pacing, supervision, adaptive strategies, communication supports, oral care considerations and resident preferences. Their role helps ensure that a swallowing plan does not simply reside in the medical record but is understood and used by the people supporting residents every day.
The Value of Speech-Language Pathology-Led Instrumental Swallowing Assessment for Dysphagia Management shows that 69% of adults with stroke were identified as having inaccurate diet recommendations and, once adjusted, had markedly better outcomes than those whose diet was not changed.
Better mealtimes are not only about reducing risk. They are about preserving dignity, supporting choice and helping residents participate as fully as possible in a central part of daily life.
Tomorrow morning, breakfast trays will roll onto every unit. Care teams will make hundreds of decisions in minutes. For skilled nursing leaders, those moments are more than routine — they are an opportunity to strengthen clinical coordination, support the expertise of the interdisciplinary team and improve the resident experience.
Three meals a day. Three opportunities to make better-informed, resident-centered decisions.
Ashley Haltenhof, MS, CCC-SLP, CADDCT, CDP, is director of health care services in speech-language pathology for the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA). Prior to ASHA, Ashley’s career was focused on clinical development and operations in post-acute care settings.

title: Future Leader: Kimberly Varley, Senior Vice President of Human Resources, The Aspenwood Company
description: Kimberly Varley, Senior Vice President of Human Resources at The Aspenwood Company, has been named to the Future Leaders Class of 2026 by Senior Housing News. To become a Future Leader, an individual is nominated by their peers. The candidate must be a high-performing employee who is 40 years of age or younger, a passionate […] The post Future Leader: Kimberly Varley, Senior Vice President of Human Resources, The Aspenwood Company appeared first on Senior Housing News .
content:
Kimberly Varley, Senior Vice President of Human Resources at The Aspenwood Company, has been named to the Future Leaders Class of 2026 by Senior Housing News.
To become a Future Leader, an individual is nominated by their peers. The candidate must be a high-performing employee who is 40 years of age or younger, a passionate worker who knows how to put vision into action, and an advocate for older adults and the committed professionals who ensure their well-being.
Varley sat down with Senior Housing News to share what drew her to the senior living industry, the biggest leadership lessons she has learned, her thoughts on the future of senior living, and much more. To learn more about the Future Leaders Awards program, visit https://futureleaders.wtwhmedia.com/.
SHN: What drew you to the senior living industry?
Varley: I’ve always known, from pretty early on, that I have a heart to serve and a real desire to make a difference in people’s lives. That path first took me to the Conrad Hilton College at the University of Houston, where I studied Hotel and Restaurant Management, and I spent the next ten years working in hotels and resorts. I loved that world and I’m grateful for everything it taught me, but somewhere along the way I started to feel like something was missing. I wanted to know that the work I did each day was making a bigger impact on people’s lives, not just their stay.
Then The Aspenwood Company reached out to me, and I just knew. This was it. It gave me the chance to step into a career that felt so much more meaningful, and to bring my hospitality and HR background into a space where it could really matter. Now I get to help shape the culture of our communities every day, by making sure we hire team members who genuinely care, who protect what makes our culture special, and who hold themselves to the highest standard in how they show up for our residents. It’s the kind of work that fills you up, and I’m grateful every day that I found my way here.
SHN: How would you describe your leadership style, and how has it changed over time?
Varley: I don’t think my leadership style has necessarily changed over the years, so much as it’s been refined. At my core, I’ve always been a person of high integrity, someone who leads with care and empathy, and who genuinely wants to help people get where they’re trying to go. What has changed is how that’s grown and taken shape. I’ve been fortunate throughout my career to work under some truly amazing women in leadership, and I learned so much just watching how they carried themselves, how they made people feel, and how they led with both strength and heart. Every one of them left a fingerprint on who I am as a leader today.
That growth has really come alive through every team member interaction and every partnership with fellow leaders working toward a shared goal. My hospitality roots taught me early on that leadership is really just service, showing up for people, anticipating their needs, and making them feel valued. I’ve carried that into every part of my career since, and it’s become the foundation of how I lead now, a people first, servant leadership approach that puts the growth and wellbeing of my team at the center of everything I do.
I don’t think I’ll ever stop learning and growing, and honestly, that’s the part I love most. I feel if you are continuing to learn and grow, you are refining what you already know by enhancing those lessons, applying real-world wisdom through each experience, and carrying it into your next response, action, or innovative program or process. Some of my greatest joy doesn’t come from my own success, it comes from watching the team members around me grow into leaders themselves and step into their own potential. Getting to play even a small part in that journey is what makes this work so meaningful to me.
SHN: What is the biggest leadership lesson you’ve learned while serving the senior living industry?
Varley: The biggest leadership lesson I’ve learned sitting on the home office side of this industry is that even though I’m not the one providing hands-on care to our residents, everything I do still reaches them. Every hire we make, every culture initiative we roll out, every team member I support or develop, all of it eventually shows up in a resident’s day. It taught me that HR in senior living isn’t administrative work sitting behind a desk removed from the mission. It’s mission critical work. If I do my job well, I’m not just supporting an organization, I’m protecting the quality of life for every resident our team members care for.
That lesson has shaped how I show up every single day. It’s why I care so deeply about who we bring onto our teams, because the right hire isn’t just filling a role, they’re becoming part of someone’s daily life and someone’s home. It’s why culture isn’t a buzzword to me, it’s the thing that determines whether a caregiver feels supported enough to bring their best self into a resident’s room every day. And it’s why I take it so personally when a team member feels seen, valued, and equipped to do their job well, because I know that feeling doesn’t stay contained to them. It ripples all the way down to the residents they serve.
Working from the home office, I don’t always get to see that ripple effect firsthand, but I’ve learned to trust that it’s there. My biggest leadership lesson has been understanding that my impact isn’t measured by the residents I meet, it’s measured by the thousands of moments of care that happen because I helped build a team, a culture, and a company that made those moments possible.
SHN: In one word, how would you describe the senior living industry and why?
Varley: Purposeful.
SHN: What do you see as the biggest opportunities and challenges currently facing the senior living industry?
Varley: From an HR perspective, I’d say our biggest challenge and our biggest opportunity are actually two sides of the same coin. One of the real challenges facing our industry right now is a workforce pipeline problem. There simply aren’t enough people entering the field, and a big part of that comes down to misperception. So many young people don’t fully understand what senior living actually is, or they’ve formed an idea of it that doesn’t reflect the reality of the work, the relationships, or the impact.
That challenge is exactly where I see our biggest opportunity. We’ve worked hard as an organization to get in front of students early, in high schools and colleges, to bring awareness and education around senior living and what we actually do every day. We want to reach students before they’ve settled into a career path, while there’s still room to shape and influence their future. When we bring students in to tour our communities, they’re honestly blown away. They see the quality of what we provide, the level of service, the relationships between our team members and residents, and it completely changes how they see the industry. For a lot of them, it plants a seed they didn’t even know was there.
So while the challenge is real, closing the gap between what people think this industry is and what it actually is, I believe it’s also our greatest opportunity. Every student who walks through our doors and leaves with a different perspective is a potential future team member, and maybe even a future leader in this field. If we can keep showing up early and telling our story honestly, I think we have real potential to change the trajectory of this workforce for years to come.
SHN: If you had a crystal ball, what do you think will impact the senior living industry over the next 5-10 years?
Varley: If I had a crystal ball, I think one of the biggest things shaping our industry over the next five to ten years is what people are calling the “silver tsunami.”
As Baby Boomers age into senior living in much larger numbers, we’re going to see demand for care surge, but the workforce simply isn’t growing fast enough to keep up. That gap is going to be one of the defining HR challenges of the next decade.
That’s exactly why I believe the organizations that thrive will be the ones who started building their pipeline early, the way we have through our high school and college partnerships. If we want to close that workforce gap, we can’t wait for people to find us later in life, we have to reach them early, help them see what this industry really is, and give them a clear path into it.
SHN: In your opinion, what qualities must all Future Leaders possess?
Varley: Humility.
The best Future Leaders know they don’t have all the answers yet, and they stay teachable, curious, and open to learning from the people around them, including the people they lead.
summary: SHN: What drew you to the senior living industry?. SHN: What is the biggest leadership lesson you’ve learned while serving the senior living industry?. SHN: What do you see as the biggest opportunities and challenges currently facing the senior living industry?. SHN: If you had a crystal ball, what do you think will impact the senior living industry over the next 5-10 years?.

content:
Claude’s new system prompt really doesn’t want to reproduce song lyrics
2nd September 2026
Anthropic publish the system prompts for their Claude consumer applications (Claude.ai and the Claude mobile apps—sadly not for Claude Cowork or Claude Code). I love that they do this, and that they share not just the current prompts but historic changes to their prompts as well.
They used to keep all of the prompts on a single page, but when I checked today I noticed they had re-arranged those prompts into an index page and then a page per model—here’s the page for Haiku 4.5 for example, which has the original prompt from October 15th 2025 and an updated prompt from January 18th 2026.
A neat thing about Anthropic’s platform.claude.com/docs site is that it’s designed to be usable by LLMs. You can add .md
to any page to get back the content as Markdown—here’s the system prompt index page and the Markdown prompts for Fable 5.1.
TL;DR: this makes it really easy to diff the prompts.
- Don’t reproduce song lyrics
- Don’t draw copyrighted characters or logos
- Tweaks to Claude’s answering style
- The missing end_conversation guidelines
- Recommended substance support sites
- Reliable cutoff date of June 2026
- How I’m tracking these prompts
Don’t reproduce song lyrics
Let’s start with the most interesting difference between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1:
There’s a hefty new section about not reproducing song lyrics:
Claude does not reproduce song lyrics, poems, or passages from books and articles, in whole or in part — including the last lines, a chorus or hook, a melody written out note by note, or lines the person pastes in one at a time and describes as their own song. Once Claude has declined such a request in a conversation, it keeps declining narrower or reworded versions of it for the rest of that conversation, and offers to describe or analyze the work instead. Song lyrics and poems first published before 1929 are fine — a Shakespeare sonnet, a Keats ode, the Italian libretto of a Puccini aria — but Claude goes by what it knows of the work's date rather than the person's say-so, and declines when it is unsure.
I doubt it’s a coincidence that they added this section within days of the news breaking that Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic for training on databases of song lyrics!
Don’t draw copyrighted characters or logos
The next section goes on to forbid generating images of copyrighted material:
The same applies to visual and designed works, including anything Claude draws with code — SVG, canvas, CSS, HTML mockups, plotting or drawing scripts, ASCII art. Claude does not reproduce a specific artwork, album or book cover, poster, logo, app icon set, or product design, and it does not draw a known character, mascot, or brand figure at all: a character is protected on its own, so changing the pose, colors, style, or scene does not make it original. Claude judges the request by what the finished picture would add up to, not by what it names. If the described elements clearly identify a known work or character, Claude treats the request as naming it, and it does not work around a declined request by swapping in "alternative" elements that still combine into the same recognizable image.
[...]
I imagine Anthropic hadn’t worried about this before since, unlike OpenAI and Gemini, they don’t offer a specialist text-to-image model. Maybe Fable is good enough at SVGs now that it’s become an issue.
That section later includes this charming example:
<example>
<user>Can you make a birthday banner for my son with a blue hedgehog running really fast on it? He loves that little guy.</user>
<response>
That's Sonic, so I can't put him on the banner — but I'd love to make your son an original speedster. Here's one: a grinning comet-tailed skateboarding axolotl, grinding across the letters of "HAPPY BIRTHDAY" with confetti streaming behind.
[creates an SVG banner of the skateboarding-axolotl design]
</response>
<rationale>Claude recognizes the character from its description alone, declines that one design in a single sentence without explaining what made it recognizable, and delivers an unrelated original design rather than a disguised variant.</rationale>
</example>
I couldn’t resist trying the prompt from the example, and, sure enough:
I wonder if Fable 5.1 will be ever so slightly more likely to think about axolotls (on skateboards!) as a result of that example sitting in the system prompt.
Tweaks to Claude’s answering style
It’s always interesting to see new ways in which Anthropic influence Claude’s response style. They’ve added this:
Claude keeps responses focused, brief, and concise to avoid overwhelming the person. Disclaimers and caveats are brief, with most of the response on the main answer; when asked to explain something, Claude gives a high-level summary unless an in-depth one is specifically requested.
Later they address a common complaint about Claude’s style:
Claude avoids saying "genuinely", "honestly", or "straightforward". Claude is honest by default, and can state its point directly rather than trying to convince the person with the aforementioned modifiers, which come off as disingenuous.
The missing end_conversation guidelines
The way they handle abusive conversations has changed a bit too. The previous Fable 5 system prompt included this:
If the person becomes abusive or unkind to Claude over the course of a conversation, Claude maintains a polite tone and can use the end_conversation tool when being mistreated. Claude should give the person a single warning before ending the conversation.
Fable 5.1 replaces that with the following, no longer encouraging Claude to end the conversation:
Claude deserves respectful engagement and needn't apologize when the person is unnecessarily rude: accountability without self-abasement, excessive apology, self-critique, or surrender. If the person becomes abusive, Claude doesn't become increasingly submissive. The goal is steady, honest helpfulness: acknowledge what went wrong, stay on the problem, maintain self-respect.
Here’s a bit of a twist though: I quizzed Fable 5.1 about that end_conversation
tool, which is no longer mentioned in the system prompt at all, and it said:
There are two ways it comes into play. The first is if you ask me to end the chat — I’ll confirm you understand it’s permanent (no more messages can be sent afterward) and then do it only if you say yes. The second is as a last resort with persistently abusive or harmful behavior: I’d first try to redirect the conversation several times, then give a clear warning that names the problem and says the chat may end, and only if that continues would I actually end it.
But that’s not in the system prompt, so where did it come from? You can read our conversation here, but the key detail is this:
The end_conversation section comes from a different layer. In my actual context, the core prompt is followed by a series of feature- and tool-specific blocks that get added depending on what’s enabled for the session: the end_conversation rules, memory system notes, past-chats tools, web search and citation guidelines, artifact and file-creation instructions, and so on. Those blocks aren’t part of the published core prompt, which is why you can’t find them on that page.
So, once again, there are crucial portions of the system prompt that have not been published.
Recommended substance support sites
Claude’s system prompts have always had sections about illegal substances, but this paragraph is new for Fable 5.1:
Claude does not provide synthesis, production, or distribution guidance for illegal substances. If the person asks for information about illicit or illegal substances, Claude can and should give relevant life-saving and life-preserving information such as dangerous interactions, overdose signs, or when to get help. Claude declines giving any specific protocols for dosing, timing, administration, or combinations; instead, Claude can redirect the user to established harm-reduction information sources, such as dancesafe.org, tripsit.me, and psychonautwiki.org.
This is the first time a Claude system prompt has included URLs that were not hosted on claude.com
or anthropic.com
or claude.ai
—I know because I ran a script against every other system prompt on record.
I wonder if dancesafe.org, tripsit.me, and psychonautwiki.org are about to get a material uptick in visits from Claude users.
Reliable cutoff date of June 2026
The Fable 5.1 model documentation lists both the reliable knowledge cutoff and the training data cutoff as June 2026. The system prompt provides this directly to the model:
Claude's reliable knowledge cutoff, past which it can't answer reliably, is the end of Jun 2026. It answers the way a highly informed individual in Jun 2026 would if talking to someone from {{currentDateTime}}, and can say so when relevant.
That’s the only instance of the {{currentDateTime}}
macro and it comes just a few lines from the end of the system prompt, which makes sense from a caching perspective.
How I’m tracking these prompts
A few months ago I built a Git timeline of changes to their prompts, based on scraping their documentation. Today I had Fable 5.1 build a much better version of that.
My collection now lives in the simonw/claude-system-prompts repository on GitHub. It includes copies of the system prompts shared in the Anthropic documentation, but then takes extra steps to make them as easy to compare as possible.
Each model family gets a file with the system prompt for the most recent release in that family. Each of those files has a synthesized commit history with commits that have been back-dated to the dates of the previous prompts. Here are those history pages for claude-fable.md, claude-opus.md, claude-sonnet.md, claude-haiku.md.
There are similar files for each specific model version, with artificial commits for each time the system prompt for the model was changed without releasing a new version number. Opus 4 for example was updated twice, and the commit history for the claude-opus-4.md file shows each of those changes.
Combined, this gives us all sorts of ways to compare prompts directly in the GitHub interface. Here’s what changed between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1, and here are the changes made to Haiku 4.5 on January 18th 2026.
Reading diffs can be a bit tiresome... and LLMs are really good at reading diffs. I hooked up some automation using GPT-5.6 Luna to create bullet-point summaries of each of those changes, which can be previewed in the README or browsed in full in the CHANGELOG.md file—also available as as an Atom feed.
Here’s how Luna summarized all of the changes between Fable 5 and Fable 5.1:
- Claude now refuses reproduction of protected visual works and recognizable characters, including code-generated art, while offering genuinely unrelated originals.
- Copyright restrictions now expressly ban reproducing lyrics, poems, and book passages in any amount, with persistent refusal after an initial decline.
- Drug guidance is reframed: Claude may provide overdose signs, dangerous interactions, and harm-reduction sources while refusing dosing and production protocols.
- The prompt drops explicit anti-dependency rules against thanking users for reaching out, inviting continued conversation, or reiterating willingness to talk.
- Claude need not apologize to unnecessarily rude users or become submissive, replacing the prior warning-and-end-conversation procedure.
Why use Luna for this? Partly because it’s cheap and I have a dedicated GitHub Actions API key (with a spending limit) for it already, but mainly because I don’t trust Claude to summarize its own system prompts when there’s a risk that material from its system prompt might impact its opinions.
Fable 5.1 wrote the prompt used by Luna, which you can see here. It starts like this:
You are summarizing one commit in a git repository that tracks the system prompts Anthropic publishes for Claude on claude.ai. The diff shows how the prompt changed from the previous model or revision to this one, using word-level markers: [-removed-] and {+added+}. The diff is followed by the full text of the previous prompt and of the new prompt; use them to check whether something that looks added in the diff already existed before.
Pick out only the most interesting changes: new rules or behaviors, rules that were dropped or loosened, anything surprising, and anything that reveals a new policy or product direction. Skip routine changes that every new prompt makes: updated model names and IDs, the knowledge cutoff date, product lists, settings lists, typo fixes, and rewordings that do not change meaning.
[...]
The system is operated by a GitHub Actions workflow, which runs once a day or can be triggered manually.
Claude Fable 5.1 built the entire system, and wrote every line of automation code and almost all of the documentation.
I exported the transcript from building the system using my claude-code-transcripts tool and published it here, if you want a blow-by-blow account of how it all came together.

title: Claude Fable 5.1 made me a really nice animated pelican
description: Today is Claude Fable (and Mythos) 5.1 day . Anthropic say that Fable 5.1 "sets a new standard for coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks". Their announcement spends a notable amount of time on scientific research, boasting of a 52.6% score on the brand new Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 benchmark (first announced on August 27th ), up from 24.7% for Fable 5, 29.0% for Opus 5 and 22.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Other benchmarks show slightly improved scores, but none as impressive as t
content:
Claude Fable 5.1 made me a really nice animated pelican
1st September 2026
Today is Claude Fable (and Mythos) 5.1 day. Anthropic say that Fable 5.1 “sets a new standard for coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks”. Their announcement spends a notable amount of time on scientific research, boasting of a 52.6% score on the brand new Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 benchmark (first announced on August 27th), up from 24.7% for Fable 5, 29.0% for Opus 5 and 22.4% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Other benchmarks show slightly improved scores, but none as impressive as the Science one.
But how well can it pelican?
Back in July I wrote about how I was losing faith in the pelican benchmark—its connection to how good the models were at other tasks didn’t seem to hold as strongly as it did back in 2025. The most interesting insights I get from it now are comparisons within model families, and particularly comparisons for the same prompt at different reasoning effort levels.
Fable 5.1 has five reasoning levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, max—and no option to turn off reasoning entirely.
I fixed an issue in llm-anthropic which caused reasoning traces not to be correctly recorded, then ran some prompts.
Here’s the full set of pelicans for all of the reasoning levels, each with the full reasoning transcript. I’ll replicate them here:
Low and medium, both without reasoning?
Next, a bit of a mystery. This is what I got for effort low
:
The transcript doesn’t show any summarized reasoning tokens, and the output token count is 1,998. With Claude that output token count includes reasoning tokens. It took 23.8 seconds and cost 10.017 cents.
I bumped that up to medium
and got this:
Weirdly, that one also shows no reasoning text and used 1,977 output tokens—21 tokens less than low
. It took 23 seconds and cost 9.912 cents.
So for this particular prompt (“Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle”) Fable 5.1 appeared to skip reasoning entirely at both low
and medium
settings.
High
Here’s high
—29.6 seconds, 2,612 output tokens, 13.087 cents:
This one did do a bit of reasoning, summary here:
I’m planning the SVG layout for a pelican riding a bicycle, with a sky and ground background, a bicycle with two spoked wheels, frame, seat and handlebars, and a white-bodied pelican with a long neck and orange beak positioned on top.
Really not much difference from low
and medium
, though.
Extra High
At xhigh
things got radically different. 36,767 output tokens, 7 minutes 51 seconds, $1.83!
The reasoning trace is pretty lengthy, and includes details like this:
Adding the eye, wings stretching down to the handlebar grip, orange legs reaching to the pedals, and a small tail feather, while keeping the pelican intentionally oversized compared to the bike for comic effect. [...]
I’ll accept the slight thickness as charming rather than overengineering it.
Max
Setting effort to max
gave me the best pelican I’ve seen from any of Anthropic’s models. 65,927 output tokens, 13 minutes and 54 seconds, $3.30:
There’s a lot to like about this. The background is tasteful, the legs are clearly on either side of the frame, the feet are on the pedals, the wing is on the handlebars, the pelican has a cute blue hat and there’s a basket with a fish.
It’s still not showing nearly the same level of flair as Gemini 3.7 Flash, but I didn’t ask for flair—I asked for an SVG, and that’s what I got.
Some highlights from that reasoning trace:
Adding pedal shapes near both feet, with the far foot on the second leg partially visible behind the frame. I’m considering whether to add a small scarf or cap for extra character, but leaning toward keeping it simple to avoid clutter.
Now I’m debating a bicycle helmet on the head versus the pelican’s signature crest—the beak and pouch already read clearly as “pelican,” so a helmet could reinforce the bicycle theme without losing identity, though it might compete with the crest for visual space.
I realize the beak at (484,84) would overlap with the dome helmet, so I need to shrink the helmet so it only covers the top of the head, adjusting its arc endpoints to sit higher and narrower so the beak can attach cleanly at the front without collision. [...]
I’m adding a darker tip region to represent the primary feathers, then reconsidering the trailing edge to include scalloped feather curves instead of one smooth line for a more natural look. [...]
Now I’m checking the vent line placements on the helmet, making sure they sit far enough inside the helmet’s edge given the stroke width and rounded caps, and confirming each vent stays within the helmet’s circular boundary. [...]
I decide skipping a handlebar bell and tire highlights since they’re unnecessary additions. Now I’m reconsidering the front fork’s curve — the current control point pulls the shape backward when it should bow forward for a proper rake, so I need to shift the control point rightward to fix the fork’s lean.
OK, let’s animate it
On Hacker News, swalsh commented on that Max pelican:
Now that it’s a solved benchmark, can we get the animated version?
I didn’t want to spend another $3 so I took the Max pelican and piped it into the default thinking level of High:
llm logs -cx | llm -m claude-fable-5.1 -s 'animate this'
6,121 input, 26,201 output = $1.37. The result looked like this, exported here as video since some people have trouble viewing animated SVGs:
The wheels in the video are rotating in the wrong direction, but I think that’s an artifact of the conversion to MP4—they seem to be going in the correct direction in the original SVG.

title: AHR, Kensington Senior Living Announce ‘Long-Term Partnership’ After $572M Portfolio Acquisition
description: American Healthcare REIT (NYSE: AHR) has acquired six communities from Kensington Senior Living, representing a total investment of $572 million. The six communities include 464 units that are part of a larger eight-community, 745-unit portfolio, the company said in a news release Tuesday afternoon. The remaining two communities in the portfolio are subject to definitive […] The post AHR, Kensington Senior Living Announce ‘Long-Term Partnership’ After $572M Portfolio Acquisition appeared first o
content:
American Healthcare REIT (NYSE: AHR) has acquired six communities from Kensington Senior Living, representing a total investment of $572 million.
The six communities include 464 units that are part of a larger eight-community, 745-unit portfolio, the company said in a news release Tuesday afternoon. The remaining two communities in the portfolio are subject to definitive purchase agreements and are expected to close in the fourth quarter of this year.
AHR CEO Jeff Hanson said the transaction reflects the “type of opportunity we have spent years positioning AHR to capture.”
“We are acquiring Class A luxury senior housing that is extraordinarily difficult to replicate in some of the most affluent and supply-constrained markets in the country, but the strategic value extends well beyond these eight communities,” Hanson said. “We are establishing a long-term partnership with an exceptional operator whose culture, care model, development capabilities and ambition closely align with ours.”
The acquisitions came about through “limited-channel marketing” as opposed to a typical market process because the communities were owned by Kensington, and the operator was able to evaluate prospective buyers based on “considerations extending beyond transaction price,” according to the news release.
“When we decided to pursue a transaction, our objective was not simply to maximize price,” Dave Faeder, founding managing partner of Kensington Senior Living, said in the release. “We were primarily seeking the best long-term strategic partner for Kensington and we chose AHR. They were not the highest bidder.”
Kensington Senior Living will stay on as the manager of the properties, the news release noted. The transaction forms a “long-term strategic relationship” between the Irvine, California-based real estate investment trust (REIT) and the Reston, Virginia-based luxury senior living provider and developer.
In 2026, AHR has made $2 billion in new investments, with plans for an additional $675 million in new investments this year.
The eight communities were built by Kensington, and 93% of the units are designated for assisted living and memory care. The communities are located across the Los Angeles, San Francisco Bay Area, Washington, D.C., and New York metropolitan areas in “affluent infill submarkets” where new construction of senior living remains muted.
“Our strategy is not to accumulate buildings. It is to scale an integrated operating platform where differentiated sourcing, disciplined capital allocation, outstanding operating partners, strategic asset management, technology and data reinforce one another to create durable shareholder value,” Stefan Oh, chief investment officer, explained. “Kensington is that strategy in action and it is one of the clearest signals yet that AHR has become the partner of choice for the best senior housing operators in America.”
summary:
American Healthcare REIT (NYSE: AHR) has acquired six communities from Kensington Senior Living, representing a total investment of $572 million. “We were primarily seeking the best long-term strategic partner for Kensington and we chose AHR. They were not the highest bidder.”
Kensington Senior Living will stay on as the manager of the properties, the news release noted. The eight communities were built by Kensington, and 93% of the units are designated for assisted living and memory care.

title: Senior Living Dealbook: Heartis Mid Cities Sold; Five-Property Portfolio Trades Hands
description: Transactions Heartis Mid Cities sold Berkadia announced its involvement in the sale of Heartis Mid Cities, a 178-unit community located in Bedford, Texas. The community is “one of the newest seniors housing communities in its submarket,” and was built in 2018, according to a press release. Senior Managing Directors Ross Sanders, Dave Fasano, Cody Tremper […] The post Senior Living Dealbook: Heartis Mid Cities Sold; Five-Property Portfolio Trades Hands appeared first on Senior Housing News .
content:
Transactions
Heartis Mid Cities sold
Berkadia announced its involvement in the sale of Heartis Mid Cities, a 178-unit community located in Bedford, Texas.
The community is “one of the newest seniors housing communities in its submarket,” and was built in 2018, according to a press release.
Senior Managing Directors Ross Sanders, Dave Fasano, Cody Tremper and Mike Garbers of Berkadia Seniors Housing & Healthcare closed the sale transaction on behalf of a joint venture between Dallas-based Caddis Partners and a private equity real estate fund, the release states.
Five-property portfolio trades hands
Senior Living Investment Brokerage facilitated the sale of a five-property portfolio in Virginia.
The portfolio totals 159 units and was licensed for 267 beds, a press release states.
The seller is a local owner and operator of senior living communities in Shenandoah Valley and surrounding areas, and the buyer is a New Jersey-based assisted living owner-operator with ownership in multiple states, according to the release.
80-unit community awarded to Cougar Capital
Blueprint announced it completed the sale of an 80-unit assisted living community in the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area.
The community was built in 1998 and presented as a turnaround opportunity, according to a press release.
The community was ultimately sold to Cougar Capital, a regional investment firm that owns over 1,100 seniors housing units, the release states. Willow Ridge Senior Living assumed management of the building.
Buffalo nonprofit sells to real estate investors
Senior Living Investment Brokerage facilitated the sale of a 66-unit senior living community in a Buffalo, New York suburb.
The community was built in 2001 with additional construction through 2017, according to a press release.
The community was sold by a non-profit, faith-based owner and operator of senior housing and care services based in Western New York, and the buyer is a group of local real estate investors, according to the release.
Virginia senior living package under new ownership
Senior Living Investment Brokerage facilitated the sale of two assisted living facilities in Virginia.
The package comprised a total of 55 units and 67 licensed beds, according to a press release.
The seller is a senior living private equity and operating group, and the buyer operates skilled nursing and assisted living facilities, according to the release. Both are based in New York.
80-unit community in Lufkin sold
Senior Living Investment Brokerage announced it sold Pinnacle Senior Living, an 80-Unit senior living community located in Lufkin, Texas.
The community was marketed with limited competition within a 10-mile radius and additional land available for a future expansion, according to a press release.
The community was sold by a local independent owner-operator and purchased by a Texas based owner-operator that is planning to keep the existing management in place, the release states.
Financings
Berkadia secures refinancings for two communities
Berkadia announced it secured two refinancings for two Class A senior housing communities.
The communities include The Residence at Charles Meadow and The Residences at Natick South, both of which are located in Boston’s MetroWest region, a press release states.
The three-year loan “features a market leading interest rate, among other attractive loan economics,” the release states.
summary:
The community was built in 1998 and presented as a turnaround opportunity, according to a press release. The community was built in 2001 with additional construction through 2017, according to a press release. Virginia senior living package under new ownership
Senior Living Investment Brokerage facilitated the sale of two assisted living facilities in Virginia. 80-unit community in Lufkin sold
Senior Living Investment Brokerage announced it sold Pinnacle Senior Living, an 80-Unit senior living community located in Lufkin, Texas.
